chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Sa'd ibn Isma'il from his father who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) about the prayer mat and carpet on which there are figures/images, whether one stands on it and prays or not. He said, 'By Allah, I dislike that.' And from a man who entered upon a man and with him was a carpet on which was a figure, he said, 'Do you find a figure here?' He said, 'Do not sit on it and do not pray on it.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report is to be understood as indicating dislike, based on the indication of the reports we have previously mentioned, and that there is no harm in sitting on it and standing on it as long as one does not prostrate on the figures, and to clarify that further is what he narrated:

key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَة: Dislike (a level of legal ruling less than prohibition)
key_terms.الْمُصَلَّى: Prayer mat or place of prostration

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pray on a carpet with images or figures on it?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the status of praying on surfaces with images, establishing the ruling as *karahat* (dislike) rather than absolute prohibition (*haram*), provided the worshipper does not prostrate directly upon the figures. Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this by distinguishing between mere presence of images and the act of bowing or prostrating on them, reflecting the Shia juristic principle of avoiding *tashabbuh* (resemblance) with idolaters without imposing undue hardship. This nuanced view allows for practical flexibility in daily prayer while maintaining spiritual purity and reverence.
